sentence: Bisoprolol is a beta blocker, a type of medicine used to treat high blood pressure and heart failure.
note: NHS: beta blocker used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and heart failure.

sentence: It is also used to prevent the chest pain caused by angina, and to treat atrial fibrillation and other conditions that cause an irregular heartbeat.
note: NHS: also used to prevent chest pain caused by angina; treat atrial fibrillation and other irregular heartbeat conditions.

sentence: It is only available on prescription.
note: NHS: only available on prescription.

sentence: The NHS says bisoprolol works as well as other beta blockers at lowering blood pressure but is less likely to cause side effects, because it acts mainly on the heart.
note: NHS: works as well as other beta blockers for reducing blood pressure, less likely to cause side effects because it works mainly on the heart.

sentence: Manufacturer leaflets say it is not recommended for children or adolescents.
note: Leaflets: not recommended for use in children or adolescents.

sentence: Because it acts mainly on the heart, bisoprolol is described as a beta blocker that is more targeted than some others.
note: NHS: works mainly on the heart; less likely to cause side effects.

sentence: Beta blockers as a group make the heart beat more slowly and with less force, which lowers blood pressure.
note: NHS beta blockers page describes slowing the heart and lowering blood pressure (search summary; wording paraphrased).

sentence: Bisoprolol comes as tablets that are swallowed whole with a drink, with or without food.
note: Leaflets: swallowed whole with a drink, may be taken with or without food.

sentence: The NHS notes that taking it after eating might help, and the prescriber or pharmacist sets how much to take and when.
note: NHS: it might help to take bisoprolol after you have eaten (search summary); dose set by prescriber (no dose given here).

sentence: If you feel dizzy or weak, the NHS advises stopping what you are doing and sitting or lying down until you feel better.
note: NHS: if you feel dizzy or weak, stop what you're doing and sit or lie down until you feel better.

sentence: The NHS lists dizziness, feeling sick, cold hands or feet, headaches, tiredness, and constipation or diarrhoea among the common side effects.
note: NHS key facts: dizziness, feeling sick, cold hands or feet, constipation or diarrhoea; headaches and tiredness listed as common.

sentence: These are usually mild and do not last for long.
note: NHS: usually mild and do not last for long.

sentence: A slow heartbeat and disturbed sleep are also described as common in other patient information, and tiredness, dizziness or lightheadedness can be signs of a slow heart rate with beta blockers.
note: NHS beta-blockers page: feeling tired, dizzy or lightheaded can be signs of a slow heart rate; another source lists slow heartbeat among common effects.

sentence: Call 999 now if you have shortness of breath, wheezing or tightness of the chest, which can be signs of lung problems.
note: NHS side effects page, 999 section: shortness of breath, wheezing, tightening of the chest; call 999 now.

sentence: Call your doctor or NHS 111 now if your skin or the whites of your eyes turn yellow, which can be a sign of liver problems.
note: NHS: yellow skin/eyes, signs of liver problems; call a doctor or 111 now.

sentence: The same advice applies to a cough and breathlessness that get worse on exercise, swollen ankles or legs, or an irregular heartbeat, which can be signs of heart problems.
note: NHS: call doctor or 111 now for breathlessness with worsening cough on exercise, swollen ankles or legs, or irregular heartbeat.

sentence: Manufacturer leaflets say that if you suddenly stop taking bisoprolol you are likely to have side effects, and that treatment should not be stopped abruptly.
note: Leaflets: suddenly stopping likely to cause side effects; should not be stopped abruptly.

sentence: Speak to the prescriber or pharmacist before stopping, so that any reduction can be planned, because leaflets describe the dose being lowered gradually.
note: Leaflets: dose should be reduced gradually; speak to prescriber before stopping.

sentence: The NHS says some medicines can interact with bisoprolol, including painkillers such as ibuprofen and antidepressants such as amitriptyline.
note: NHS interactions page (search summary): painkillers such as ibuprofen and antidepressants such as amitriptyline.

sentence: Leaflets also mention certain medicines for heart rhythm problems and treatments for clinical shock.
note: Leaflets: certain antiarrhythmic drugs and treatments for clinical shock.

sentence: The NHS advises telling a doctor or pharmacist about everything you take, including herbal supplements.
note: NHS page title and summary: other medicines and herbal supplements; tell your doctor or pharmacist about everything you take.

sentence: Alcohol can increase the blood-pressure-lowering effect of bisoprolol, which can leave you feeling dizzy or lightheaded.
note: NHS: drinking alcohol can increase the blood pressure-lowering effect, can make you feel dizzy or lightheaded.

sentence: The NHS suggests avoiding alcohol at the start of treatment or after a change in the amount you take, until you see how the medicine affects you.
note: NHS: avoid alcohol at the start of treatment or after a dose increase until you see how it affects you.

sentence: The NHS lists people who have had an allergic reaction to bisoprolol or another beta blocker, and people with conditions such as asthma, low blood pressure, diabetes, kidney disease or peripheral arterial disease, as needing to check with a doctor or pharmacist first.
note: NHS who-can-and-cannot-take summary: previous allergic reaction to beta blocker; breathing problems such as asthma, low blood pressure, diabetes, kidney disease, peripheral arterial disease.

sentence: NHS-linked patient information says beta blockers may make asthma worse, so they may not be suitable.
note: NHS-affiliated guides: beta blockers not suitable for people with a breathing problem such as asthma or COPD; may make asthma worse.

sentence: In diabetes, bisoprolol may make the warning signs of low blood sugar harder to recognise.
note: NHS medicines page: may make it more difficult to recognise warning signs of low blood sugar.

sentence: The NHS says bisoprolol can be taken during pregnancy, but you and your baby may be offered extra checks.
note: NHS: can be taken during pregnancy, extra checks may be offered.

sentence: Taking it while breastfeeding may cause side effects in the baby, so tell the prescriber if you are pregnant, planning a pregnancy or breastfeeding.
note: NHS: breastfeeding may cause side effects in baby.

sentence: Some manufacturer leaflets are stricter about pregnancy than the NHS, so the leaflet for your own product is worth reading.
note: Search summary: some manufacturer leaflets say not to use during pregnancy; check specific product leaflet.

sentence: Tiredness is listed by the NHS as a common side effect of bisoprolol.
note: NHS lists headaches, tiredness as common side effects.

sentence: Feeling tired, dizzy or lightheaded can also be signs of a slow heart rate with beta blockers, so if it troubles you, speak to your GP or pharmacist.
note: NHS beta blockers: tired, dizzy, lightheaded can be signs of slow heart rate.

sentence: If you feel dizzy or weak, sitting or lying down until it passes is the NHS advice.
note: NHS: sit or lie down until you feel better.

sentence: Leaflets say stopping bisoprolol suddenly is likely to cause side effects and treatment should not be stopped abruptly.
note: Leaflets: suddenly stop likely side effects.

sentence: Leaflets describe the dose being lowered gradually when treatment does need to end.
note: Leaflets: dose should be reduced gradually.

sentence: Talk to the prescriber first, who can explain whether and how to reduce it.
note: Leaflets: speak to prescriber.

sentence: Breathing problems are listed among the serious side effects of bisoprolol.
note: NHS lists breathing problems as a serious side effect.

sentence: The NHS says shortness of breath, wheezing or chest tightness need a 999 call.
note: NHS: call 999 now for shortness of breath, wheezing, tightening of chest.

sentence: People with asthma should check with a doctor or pharmacist before taking a beta blocker, as it may make asthma worse.
note: NHS: asthma listed under care; NHS-affiliated guides say may make asthma worse.
